Among 264 Q13 respondents, reported net differences between proportions saying each area was more versus less important for newsroom focus in the era of AI were +91 for original investigations/on-the-ground reporting, +82 for contextual analysis (explanation, framing), and −42 for service journalism; these are perceptions of importance, not newsroom behavior.
Among 263 Q19 respondents, 70% were somewhat or very concerned about creators taking time and attention away from publisher content, compared with 39% concerned about losing talent.

Among 265 Q11 respondents, the adjective closest to describing the impact of newsroom AI initiatives so far was “promising” for 44%, “limited” for 42%, “transformational” for 13%, and “disappointing” for 2%.

Publisher respondents (base 272) express varied expectations for possible AI-company licensing deals around news-content IP in about three years: 69% expect at least some income, comprising 49% expecting a minor source and 20% a significant source; 20% expect no income, 11% do not know, and 0% expect a main source.

Among respondents from commercial publishers excluding publicly funded public broadcasters (base 259), 37% expect funding from platforms, including AI platforms, to be likely important or very important for their company in 2026; the chart annotates this as up 17 percentage points in the last two years, driven by new AI revenues.

selected_themes: Search signals differ in status: aggregate Chartbeat data show Google organic-search traffic to more than 2,500 sites fell 33% globally from November 2024 to November 2025, while the average slider score among 268 Q5 respondents indicates an expectation of declining search-engine traffic over the next three years, not an observed change.

Among 264 Q13 respondents, reported net differences between proportions saying each area was more versus less important for newsroom focus in the era of AI were +91 for original investigations/on-the-ground reporting, +82 for contextual analysis (explanation, framing), and −42 for service journalism; these are perceptions of importance, not newsroom behavior.
Among 263 Q19 respondents, 70% were somewhat or very concerned about creators taking time and attention away from publisher content, compared with 39% concerned about losing talent.

Among 265 Q11 respondents, the adjective closest to describing the impact of newsroom AI initiatives so far was “promising” for 44%, “limited” for 42%, “transformational” for 13%, and “disappointing” for 2%.

Publisher respondents (base 272) express varied expectations for possible AI-company licensing deals around news-content IP in about three years: 69% expect at least some income, comprising 49% expecting a minor source and 20% a significant source; 20% expect no income, 11% do not know, and 0% expect a main source.

Among respondents from commercial publishers excluding publicly funded public broadcasters (base 259), 37% expect funding from platforms, including AI platforms, to be likely important or very important for their company in 2026; the chart annotates this as up 17 percentage points in the last two years, driven by new AI revenues.

claim_ledgers.claim_text: Google organic-search traffic to more than 2,500 sites fell 33% globally from November 2024 to November 2025.
For Q5, the 268 respondents’ average slider score was −43% on a slider ranging from +100% to −100%, indicating an expectation of declining search-engine traffic over the next three years.

Among the 264 Q13 respondents, the reported net differences between proportions saying each area was more versus less important for newsroom focus in the era of AI were +91 for original investigations/on-the-ground reporting, +82 for contextual analysis (explanation, framing), and −42 for service journalism.
Among Q11 respondents (base 265), 44% chose promising and 42% limited as the adjective closest to describing the impact of newsroom AI initiatives so far.

Among publisher respondents (base 272), 69% expect possible licensing deals with AI companies around news-content IP to bring at least some income to their company in about three years: 49% expect a minor source and 20% a significant source.

Chartbeat aggregate data sourced for the report show Google traffic from organic search to more than 2,500 sites fell 33% globally between November 2024 and November 2025. Separately, the average slider score among Q5 respondents (base 268; slider range +100% to −100%) was −43% for expected search-engine traffic change over the next three years, an expectation rather than an observed change.

Among the 264 Q13 respondents, the reported net difference between proportions saying areas were more versus less important for newsroom focus in the era of AI was +91 for original investigations/on-the-ground reporting, +82 for contextual analysis (explanation, framing), and −42 for service journalism.
Among respondents to Q19 (base 263), 70% were somewhat or very concerned about creators taking time and attention away from publisher content, compared with 39% concerned about losing talent.

Among respondents answering Q11 (base = 265), 44% chose promising, 42% limited, 13% transformational, and 2% disappointing as the adjective closest to describing the impact of newsroom AI initiatives so far.

Among publisher respondents (base 272), 69% expect possible licensing deals with AI companies around news-content IP to bring at least some money to their company in about three years: 49% expect a minor source and 20% a significant source. Separately, 20% expect no income, 11% don't know, and 0% expect a main source of income.

Among respondents from commercial publishers, excluding publicly funded public broadcasters (base 259), 37% said funding from platforms, including AI platforms, was likely to be important or very important for their company in 2026. The chart also marks this as up +17 percentage points in the last two years, driven by new AI revenues.

editorial_plan.report_thesis: The evidence presents a decision picture spanning observed and anticipated search pressure, stated newsroom content priorities and creator concerns, and prospective platform/AI revenue alongside assessments of current newsroom AI initiatives.

themes.theme: Search signals differ in status: aggregate Chartbeat data show Google organic-search traffic to more than 2,500 sites fell 33% globally from November 2024 to November 2025, while the average slider score among 268 Q5 respondents indicates an expectation of declining search-engine traffic over the next three years, not an observed change.

Among 264 Q13 respondents, reported net differences between proportions saying each area was more versus less important for newsroom focus in the era of AI were +91 for original investigations/on-the-ground reporting, +82 for contextual analysis (explanation, framing), and −42 for service journalism; these are perceptions of importance, not newsroom behavior.
Among 263 Q19 respondents, 70% were somewhat or very concerned about creators taking time and attention away from publisher content, compared with 39% concerned about losing talent.

Among 265 Q11 respondents, the adjective closest to describing the impact of newsroom AI initiatives so far was “promising” for 44%, “limited” for 42%, “transformational” for 13%, and “disappointing” for 2%.

Publisher respondents (base 272) express varied expectations for possible AI-company licensing deals around news-content IP in about three years: 69% expect at least some income, comprising 49% expecting a minor source and 20% a significant source; 20% expect no income, 11% do not know, and 0% expect a main source.

Among respondents from commercial publishers excluding publicly funded public broadcasters (base 259), 37% expect funding from platforms, including AI platforms, to be likely important or very important for their company in 2026; the chart annotates this as up 17 percentage points in the last two years, driven by new AI revenues.

decision_implications: The observed decline and respondent expectation are different signals; use them as separate inputs to traffic scenarios.
The stated priorities provide a directional signal, not evidence that newsroom practice has changed.
The greater reported concern is attention diversion, not talent loss; treat them as distinct creator-strategy questions.

artifacts_payload.linkedin_post:
Google organic-search traffic to more than 2,500 sites fell 33% globally between November 2024 and November 2025, according to aggregate Chartbeat data sourced for the report.

This is an observed historical change in Google organic-search traffic, not a forecast.

MarketLense’s advice: when updating acquisition scenarios, keep observed referral data tied to its channel, geography and period.

summary.executive_summary: Chartbeat aggregate data show Google traffic from organic search to more than 2,500 sites fell 33% globally from November 2024 to November 2025. For Q5, the 268 respondents’ average slider score was −43% on a slider ranging from +100% to −100%, indicating an expectation of declining search-engine traffic over the next three years. Among the 264 Q13 respondents, the reported net differences between proportions saying each area was more versus less important for newsroom focus in the era of AI were +91 for original investigations/on-the-ground reporting, +82 for contextual analysis (explanation, framing), and −42 for service journalism. Among Q11 respondents (base 265), 44% chose promising and 42% limited as the adjective closest to describing the impact of newsroom AI initiatives so far. Among publisher respondents (base 272), 69% expect possible licensing deals with AI companies around news-content IP to bring at least some income to their company in about three years: 49% expect a minor source and 20% a significant source.
summary.tldr: Chartbeat aggregate data show Google traffic from organic search to more than 2,500 sites fell 33% globally from November 2024 to November 2025.

source_truth_notes_by_page.12: The page states that publishers expect search-engine traffic to almost halve (−43%) over the next three years. The adjacent chart labels −43% as the “Average score,” and its Q5 prompt asks how traffic from search engines might have changed in three years; the prompt gives a base of 268 and notes the slider range of +100% to −100%. These support the claim as a respondent expectation, not an observed change. No geography is specified for this survey measure.

verified_facts.statement: For Q5, the 268 respondents’ average slider score was −43%, indicating an expectation that traffic from search engines would decline over the next three years; this is an expectation, not an observed traffic change.

source_truth_notes_by_page.15: The chart's labels directly pair 20% with 'Significant source of income' and 49% with 'Minor source of income'; a bracket groups those categories under '69% think there will be at least some money.' The remaining labeled responses are 20% 'We won't be getting any income,' 11% 'Don't know,' and 0% 'Main source of income.' The accompanying question specifies possible licensing deals with AI companies around news content IP, income to the respondent's company in about three years, and Base = 272. Thus the reported percentages describe respondents' expectations, not realized income.

qualifiers: The chart reports publisher expectations, not realized income.
The question concerns possible licensing deals with AI companies around news-content IP and asks about the money's significance to respondents' companies.

verified_facts.statement: Among publisher respondents (base 272), 69% think possible licensing deals with AI companies around news-content IP will bring at least some money to their company in about three years: 49% expect a minor source of income and 20% a significant source. Another 20% expect no income, 11% don't know, and 0% expect it to be a main source of income.

selected_themes: Search signals differ in status: aggregate Chartbeat data show Google organic-search traffic to more than 2,500 sites fell 33% globally from November 2024 to November 2025, while the average slider score among 268 Q5 respondents indicates an expectation of declining search-engine traffic over the next three years, not an observed change.

Among 264 Q13 respondents, reported net differences between proportions saying each area was more versus less important for newsroom focus in the era of AI were +91 for original investigations/on-the-ground reporting, +82 for contextual analysis (explanation, framing), and −42 for service journalism; these are perceptions of importance, not newsroom behavior.
Among 263 Q19 respondents, 70% were somewhat or very concerned about creators taking time and attention away from publisher content, compared with 39% concerned about losing talent.

Among 265 Q11 respondents, the adjective closest to describing the impact of newsroom AI initiatives so far was “promising” for 44%, “limited” for 42%, “transformational” for 13%, and “disappointing” for 2%.

Publisher respondents (base 272) express varied expectations for possible AI-company licensing deals around news-content IP in about three years: 69% expect at least some income, comprising 49% expecting a minor source and 20% a significant source; 20% expect no income, 11% do not know, and 0% expect a main source.

Among respondents from commercial publishers excluding publicly funded public broadcasters (base 259), 37% expect funding from platforms, including AI platforms, to be likely important or very important for their company in 2026; the chart annotates this as up 17 percentage points in the last two years, driven by new AI revenues.

claim_ledgers.claim_text: Google organic-search traffic to more than 2,500 sites fell 33% globally from November 2024 to November 2025.
For Q5, the 268 respondents’ average slider score was −43% on a slider ranging from +100% to −100%, indicating an expectation of declining search-engine traffic over the next three years.

Among the 264 Q13 respondents, the reported net differences between proportions saying each area was more versus less important for newsroom focus in the era of AI were +91 for original investigations/on-the-ground reporting, +82 for contextual analysis (explanation, framing), and −42 for service journalism.
Among Q11 respondents (base 265), 44% chose promising and 42% limited as the adjective closest to describing the impact of newsroom AI initiatives so far.

Among publisher respondents (base 272), 69% expect possible licensing deals with AI companies around news-content IP to bring at least some income to their company in about three years: 49% expect a minor source and 20% a significant source.

Chartbeat aggregate data sourced for the report show Google traffic from organic search to more than 2,500 sites fell 33% globally between November 2024 and November 2025. Separately, the average slider score among Q5 respondents (base 268; slider range +100% to −100%) was −43% for expected search-engine traffic change over the next three years, an expectation rather than an observed change.

Among the 264 Q13 respondents, the reported net difference between proportions saying areas were more versus less important for newsroom focus in the era of AI was +91 for original investigations/on-the-ground reporting, +82 for contextual analysis (explanation, framing), and −42 for service journalism.
Among respondents to Q19 (base 263), 70% were somewhat or very concerned about creators taking time and attention away from publisher content, compared with 39% concerned about losing talent.

Among respondents answering Q11 (base = 265), 44% chose promising, 42% limited, 13% transformational, and 2% disappointing as the adjective closest to describing the impact of newsroom AI initiatives so far.

Among publisher respondents (base 272), 69% expect possible licensing deals with AI companies around news-content IP to bring at least some money to their company in about three years: 49% expect a minor source and 20% a significant source. Separately, 20% expect no income, 11% don't know, and 0% expect a main source of income.

Among respondents from commercial publishers, excluding publicly funded public broadcasters (base 259), 37% said funding from platforms, including AI platforms, was likely to be important or very important for their company in 2026. The chart also marks this as up +17 percentage points in the last two years, driven by new AI revenues.

cover_semantics.selection_reason: The evidence is metric-rich and led by a documented global search-traffic decline, alongside survey measures of priorities, assessments, and expectations.

editorial_plan.report_thesis: The evidence presents a decision picture spanning observed and anticipated search pressure, stated newsroom content priorities and creator concerns, and prospective platform/AI revenue alongside assessments of current newsroom AI initiatives.

themes.theme: Search signals differ in status: aggregate Chartbeat data show Google organic-search traffic to more than 2,500 sites fell 33% globally from November 2024 to November 2025, while the average slider score among 268 Q5 respondents indicates an expectation of declining search-engine traffic over the next three years, not an observed change.

Among 264 Q13 respondents, reported net differences between proportions saying each area was more versus less important for newsroom focus in the era of AI were +91 for original investigations/on-the-ground reporting, +82 for contextual analysis (explanation, framing), and −42 for service journalism; these are perceptions of importance, not newsroom behavior.
Among 263 Q19 respondents, 70% were somewhat or very concerned about creators taking time and attention away from publisher content, compared with 39% concerned about losing talent.

Among 265 Q11 respondents, the adjective closest to describing the impact of newsroom AI initiatives so far was “promising” for 44%, “limited” for 42%, “transformational” for 13%, and “disappointing” for 2%.

Publisher respondents (base 272) express varied expectations for possible AI-company licensing deals around news-content IP in about three years: 69% expect at least some income, comprising 49% expecting a minor source and 20% a significant source; 20% expect no income, 11% do not know, and 0% expect a main source.

Among respondents from commercial publishers excluding publicly funded public broadcasters (base 259), 37% expect funding from platforms, including AI platforms, to be likely important or very important for their company in 2026; the chart annotates this as up 17 percentage points in the last two years, driven by new AI revenues.

decision_implications: The observed decline and respondent expectation are different signals; use them as separate inputs to traffic scenarios.
The stated priorities provide a directional signal, not evidence that newsroom practice has changed.
The greater reported concern is attention diversion, not talent loss; treat them as distinct creator-strategy questions.

artifacts.expert_comment: Chartbeat aggregate data sourced for the report show Google organic-search traffic to more than 2,500 sites fell 33% globally between November 2024 and November 2025. For Q5, the average slider score among 268 respondents was −43%, indicating an expectation of declining search-engine traffic over the next three years, not an observed change. Among 264 Q13 respondents, the reported net difference between proportions saying an area was more versus less important for newsroom focus in the era of AI was +91 points for original investigations/on-the-ground reporting, +82 for contextual analysis (explanation, framing), and −42 for service journalism; these are stated perceptions, not evidence of changed newsroom behavior. For planning, MarketLense recommends keeping observed search traffic, respondents’ search expectations, and stated content priorities as separate inputs rather than treating stated priorities as evidence that newsroom practice has shifted.

summary.executive_summary: Chartbeat aggregate data show Google traffic from organic search to more than 2,500 sites fell 33% globally from November 2024 to November 2025. For Q5, the 268 respondents’ average slider score was −43% on a slider ranging from +100% to −100%, indicating an expectation of declining search-engine traffic over the next three years. Among the 264 Q13 respondents, the reported net differences between proportions saying each area was more versus less important for newsroom focus in the era of AI were +91 for original investigations/on-the-ground reporting, +82 for contextual analysis (explanation, framing), and −42 for service journalism. Among Q11 respondents (base 265), 44% chose promising and 42% limited as the adjective closest to describing the impact of newsroom AI initiatives so far. doc_map.publisher: Reuters Institute for the Study of Journalism

key_points: Newman is a Senior Research Associate at the Reuters Institute for the Study of Journalism.
He was a founding member of the BBC News Website and later led product development for BBC Journalism sites.
sections.summary: Introduces Nic Newman and his work in digital media and journalism. It notes his role at the Reuters Institute and his experience in BBC digital journalism and media strategy.
sections.title: About the Author

key_points: The report thanks 280 news executives from 51 countries and territories for responding to the survey.
The author credits Institute colleagues and other publishers, academics, and industry experts for their input.
sections.summary: Thanks survey participants, Institute colleagues, and experts who contributed ideas, interviews, and background input. The acknowledgements also continue with a list of additional contributors later in the report.
sections.title: Acknowledgements

key_points: Among surveyed leaders, 38% were confident about journalism’s prospects, compared with 53% confident about their own business prospects.
Publishers expect search-engine traffic to fall by more than 40% over the next three years; the report also notes past referral declines from Facebook and X.

For 2026, publishers favor original investigations and on-the-ground reporting (+91 net difference between those planning more and less effort), while planning greater investment in video (+79) and audio (+71).
Back-end automation was considered important by 97% of publisher respondents; 44% described newsroom AI results as promising and 42% as limited.
sections.summary: Frames Generative AI and personality-led news as major forces reshaping journalism, while describing threats from political pressure, low trust, and declining referrals. It summarizes survey findings and introduces forecast terms including AEO, digital provenance, and liquid content.
sections.title: Executive Summary

key_points: The section discusses laws and political actions that make it harder or more dangerous for journalists to operate, and efforts to label legitimate journalism as “fake news.”
Public service media face disputes over impartiality, political pressure, and proposed funding reductions.
Some mostly subscription-based publishers, particularly in Northern Europe and North America, report stronger financial and audience performance.
The forecast anticipates politicians expanding their owned-media presence, potentially through podcasts and YouTube shows.
sections.summary: Describes political attacks, legal pressure, and challenges to public service media alongside concerns about press freedom and journalism’s public standing. It also notes that some subscription-based publishers remain optimistic and predicts politicians will further strengthen their direct media presence.
sections.title: 1. Pressures on Journalism Mount

key_points: For the charted question on expected search traffic in three years, publishers’ average expectation was a 43% loss; around one-fifth expected losses greater than 75%, while some expected a decline under 20% (printed p. 10).

In the chart “Number of referrals to publisher sites in the global Chartbeat network,” global year-on-year changes from November 2024 to November 2025 were Google Search −33%, Google Discover −21%, Facebook +9%, and X +15% (printed p. 11).

The section says major AI-content deals have chiefly involved upmarket publishers and news agencies, raising concerns that local and independent outlets may be left out; survey responses on expected AI-platform income range from 20% expecting a significant contribution to 20% expecting none (printed p. 13).
The report expects more agencies, specialist consultancies, and analytics tools to offer services for Answer Engine Optimization and Generative Engine Optimization.
sections.summary: Examines how AI-generated answers and search interfaces could reduce publisher traffic, while noting that current referral changes vary by publisher and content type. It considers possible licensing arrangements and the growth of answer-engine optimization services.
sections.title: 2. Answer Engines and the Implications for Access

key_points: In “Publisher perceptions on how content needs to be refocused in the era of AI,” net difference between respondents planning more versus less effort was +91 for original investigations/on-the-ground reporting, +82 for contextual analysis, and +76 for community building (printed p. 15).
In the same chart and measure, service journalism was −42, evergreen content −32, and general news −38 (printed p. 15).

The section presents Newsquest’s AI-assisted reporters and Velora Cycling’s one-person AI-supported operation as examples of automation at scale, contrasting these with a strategy based on human distinctiveness.
sections.summary: Argues that publishers are responding to AI by emphasizing journalism that is distinctive, human, and difficult to reproduce, while reducing emphasis on content that chatbots can readily supply. It contrasts this approach with examples of highly automated publishing models.
sections.title: 3. Content Strategies Shift towards Distinctiveness

key_points: The section reports that only 17% of time spent on Facebook and 7% on Instagram involved content from friends and family, with much of the rest spent on recommended content and video (printed p. 18).
The report says average news-site referrals from Facebook fell 43% and from X fell 46% over the previous two and a half years (printed p. 18).

In “Where publishers plan to put more and less effort in 2026,” the net difference between plans for more and less effort was +74 for YouTube, +61 for AI platforms, and +56 for TikTok (printed p. 19).
sections.summary: Describes the shift from social sharing toward recommendation-driven feeds, video, and private messaging, and the resulting pressure on publisher referrals. It outlines publishers’ changing platform priorities and growing investment in video formats.
sections.title: 4. Social Media’s Mid-Life Crisis and the Video-fication of Everything

key_points: For the Q19 measure of respondents somewhat or very concerned, 70% cited creators taking time and attention away from publisher content, compared with 39% concerned about losing talent (printed p. 22).

In “Top planned publisher initiatives in response to the creator wave,” 76% planned to encourage journalists to behave more like creators, 50% to partner with creators for distribution, and 31% to hire creators (printed p. 23).
The section describes the risk that journalists who build independent profiles may leave with their audiences, including the example of former Washington Post creator Dave Jorgenson.
sections.summary: Explores creators as competitors for audience attention and editorial talent, while noting that publishers are also learning from creator-led approaches. It describes plans to adapt staff, partnerships, hiring, and studio models in response.
sections.title: 5. Responding to the Creator Wave

key_points: In “Publisher perceptions about whether misinformation and expansion of AI-generated content strengthen or weaken news media,” 52% said these trends could strengthen news media, 27% said weaken, and 15% said make no difference (printed p. 28).

The report says fewer than 1% of news images or videos published globally included C2PA metadata, and notes that TikTok’s automated detection may identify less than half of AI-generated content (printed p. 28).

The section describes more than 4,000 AI-powered fake news websites identified in France and cites a survey finding that four in ten respondents had encountered low-quality AI-generated workplace material during the previous month (printed p. 29).
sections.summary: Reviews the spread of AI-generated content and the use of manipulated media in political contexts, alongside uncertainty about the effects on trust and democracy. It discusses provenance standards, platform detection and labeling, AI content farms, and low-quality AI-generated workplace material.
sections.title: 6. AI Slop, Deep-Fakes, and Misinformation

key_points: In “Different uses of AI that will be important in 2026,” the share rating each use “very important” was 64% for back-end automation, 44% for coding and product development, 36% for distribution and recommendations, 33% for commercial uses, and 29% each for newsgathering and human-supervised content creation (printed p. 30).
In the chart on the impact of current newsroom AI initiatives, 44% described results as promising, 42% as limited, and 13% as transformational (printed p. 31).
In the chart on jobs saved or added as a result of AI initiatives, 67% reported no jobs cut, 16% a small number cut, and 9% jobs added (printed p. 31).
sections.summary: Examines publishers’ adoption of AI for efficiency and journalistic work, alongside concerns about chatbot accuracy and uneven results from newsroom initiatives. Examples include automation, coding, newsgathering, and AI-supported reporting and product development.
sections.title: 7. Latest Tales of AI in the Newsroom

key_points: In “Most important expected commercial publisher revenue streams in 2026,” the shares selecting subscription/membership, display advertising/sponsorship, native advertising, and events were 76%, 68%, 64%, and 54%, respectively (printed p. 36).
In the same chart, 37% selected funding from platforms, including AI platforms; the report notes this had risen 17 percentage points in two years (printed p. 36).
The section identifies lack of resources (62%), lack of skills (53% net), and internal competition between groups (49%) as barriers to innovation.
Predictions include further mergers and acquisitions and experimentation with community-participation models for local news.
sections.summary: Reviews pressures on established revenue models, publishers’ expectations for commercial income, and barriers to developing new products. It also considers consolidation and new approaches to local news.
sections.title: 8. Changing Business Models and Barriers to Innovation

key_points: In “Expected impact of new browsers and agentic apps,” respondents assessed impact over the next three years: 15% expected a very large impact and 60% a large impact on publishers (printed p. 39).
The report describes AI browsers and apps that can summarize or translate webpages, complete tasks, and assemble personalized news briefings.
It argues that more liquid content and agentic bots may make it harder to control how stories appear and to measure human visits.
sections.summary: Considers rapid change in AI browsers, agentic apps, and interfaces, and the implications of increasingly adaptable content for publishers’ control, measurement, and monetization. The section also raises the possibility of a stronger backlash against technology.
sections.title: 9. What’s Next in Technology?

sections.summary: The report’s concluding section closes its discussion of journalism and technology trends for 2026.
sections.title: 10. Conclusions

key_points: A closed online survey was completed by 280 senior publishing-industry participants from 51 countries and territories between 18 November and 20 December 2025 (printed p. 43).

Participants held editorial, commercial, or product roles and were responsible for aspects of digital or wider media strategy; the report cautions that the results are not representative of the wider industry.
sections.summary: Explains the survey sample and collection period, emphasizing that the responses reflect a strategic group of senior industry leaders rather than a representative sample. It also summarizes participant roles, organization types, and geographic coverage.
sections.title: Survey Methodology

doc_map.summary: Nic Newman’s report examines the pressures facing journalism and publishers in 2026, including AI-driven changes to search and content, competition from creators, platform shifts, misinformation, newsroom AI adoption, and business-model challenges. It draws on a survey of senior digital leaders and combines survey results with analysis and predictions for the year ahead.

findings.evidence:
There are many other barriers to innovation. Six in ten (62%) of our respondents say that media companies simply aren’t investing enough in future models, citing lack of resources. There is also a skills problem, with around half (53%) identifying challenges in either attracting product people who can help define the right solutions, or the technical and design talent to deliver them.

The other big problem identified by our survey is alignment. Around a quarter (26%) think the top-level strategy is not sufficiently clear, with half (49%) complaining about internal competition between different groups which makes it hard to align different parts of the organisation around new projects.

report_context.overview: Journalism and Technology Trends and Predictions 2026 by Reuters Institute for the Study of Journalism Nic Newman’s report examines the pressures facing journalism and publishers in 2026, including AI-driven changes to search and content, competition from creators, platform shifts, misinformation, newsroom AI adoption, and business-model challenges. It draws on a survey of senior digital leaders and combines survey results with analysis and predictions for the year ahead. Covers journalism and technology trends, challenges, and predictions for 2026, including AI, audience traffic, content and distribution strategies, misinformation, newsroom practices, and business models. Draws on an industry survey of digital leaders from 51 countries and territories; the excerpts do not identify specific geographic regions.

insights: Chartbeat aggregate data sourced for the report show Google traffic from organic search to more than 2,500 sites fell 33% globally between November 2024 and November 2025. Separately, the average slider score among Q5 respondents (base 268; slider range +100% to −100%) was −43% for expected search-engine traffic change over the next three years, an expectation rather than an observed change.

Among the 264 Q13 respondents, the reported net difference between proportions saying areas were more versus less important for newsroom focus in the era of AI was +91 for original investigations/on-the-ground reporting, +82 for contextual analysis (explanation, framing), and −42 for service journalism.
Among respondents to Q19 (base 263), 70% were somewhat or very concerned about creators taking time and attention away from publisher content, compared with 39% concerned about losing talent.

Among respondents answering Q11 (base = 265), 44% chose promising, 42% limited, 13% transformational, and 2% disappointing as the adjective closest to describing the impact of newsroom AI initiatives so far.

Among publisher respondents (base 272), 69% expect possible licensing deals with AI companies around news-content IP to bring at least some money to their company in about three years: 49% expect a minor source and 20% a significant source. Separately, 20% expect no income, 11% don't know, and 0% expect a main source of income.

doc_map.publisher: Reuters Institute for the Study of Journalism

key_points: Newman is a Senior Research Associate at the Reuters Institute for the Study of Journalism.
He was a founding member of the BBC News Website and later led product development for BBC Journalism sites.
sections.summary: Introduces Nic Newman and his work in digital media and journalism. It notes his role at the Reuters Institute and his experience in BBC digital journalism and media strategy.
sections.title: About the Author

key_points: The report thanks 280 news executives from 51 countries and territories for responding to the survey.
The author credits Institute colleagues and other publishers, academics, and industry experts for their input.
sections.summary: Thanks survey participants, Institute colleagues, and experts who contributed ideas, interviews, and background input. The acknowledgements also continue with a list of additional contributors later in the report.
sections.title: Acknowledgements

key_points: Among surveyed leaders, 38% were confident about journalism’s prospects, compared with 53% confident about their own business prospects.
Publishers expect search-engine traffic to fall by more than 40% over the next three years; the report also notes past referral declines from Facebook and X.

For 2026, publishers favor original investigations and on-the-ground reporting (+91 net difference between those planning more and less effort), while planning greater investment in video (+79) and audio (+71).
Back-end automation was considered important by 97% of publisher respondents; 44% described newsroom AI results as promising and 42% as limited.
sections.summary: Frames Generative AI and personality-led news as major forces reshaping journalism, while describing threats from political pressure, low trust, and declining referrals. It summarizes survey findings and introduces forecast terms including AEO, digital provenance, and liquid content.
sections.title: Executive Summary

key_points: The section discusses laws and political actions that make it harder or more dangerous for journalists to operate, and efforts to label legitimate journalism as “fake news.”
Public service media face disputes over impartiality, political pressure, and proposed funding reductions.
Some mostly subscription-based publishers, particularly in Northern Europe and North America, report stronger financial and audience performance.
The forecast anticipates politicians expanding their owned-media presence, potentially through podcasts and YouTube shows.
sections.summary: Describes political attacks, legal pressure, and challenges to public service media alongside concerns about press freedom and journalism’s public standing. It also notes that some subscription-based publishers remain optimistic and predicts politicians will further strengthen their direct media presence.
sections.title: 1. Pressures on Journalism Mount

key_points: For the charted question on expected search traffic in three years, publishers’ average expectation was a 43% loss; around one-fifth expected losses greater than 75%, while some expected a decline under 20% (printed p. 10).

In the chart “Number of referrals to publisher sites in the global Chartbeat network,” global year-on-year changes from November 2024 to November 2025 were Google Search −33%, Google Discover −21%, Facebook +9%, and X +15% (printed p. 11).

The section says major AI-content deals have chiefly involved upmarket publishers and news agencies, raising concerns that local and independent outlets may be left out; survey responses on expected AI-platform income range from 20% expecting a significant contribution to 20% expecting none (printed p. 13).
The report expects more agencies, specialist consultancies, and analytics tools to offer services for Answer Engine Optimization and Generative Engine Optimization.
sections.summary: Examines how AI-generated answers and search interfaces could reduce publisher traffic, while noting that current referral changes vary by publisher and content type. It considers possible licensing arrangements and the growth of answer-engine optimization services.
sections.title: 2. Answer Engines and the Implications for Access

key_points: In “Publisher perceptions on how content needs to be refocused in the era of AI,” net difference between respondents planning more versus less effort was +91 for original investigations/on-the-ground reporting, +82 for contextual analysis, and +76 for community building (printed p. 15).
In the same chart and measure, service journalism was −42, evergreen content −32, and general news −38 (printed p. 15).

The section presents Newsquest’s AI-assisted reporters and Velora Cycling’s one-person AI-supported operation as examples of automation at scale, contrasting these with a strategy based on human distinctiveness.
sections.summary: Argues that publishers are responding to AI by emphasizing journalism that is distinctive, human, and difficult to reproduce, while reducing emphasis on content that chatbots can readily supply. It contrasts this approach with examples of highly automated publishing models.
sections.title: 3. Content Strategies Shift towards Distinctiveness

key_points: The section reports that only 17% of time spent on Facebook and 7% on Instagram involved content from friends and family, with much of the rest spent on recommended content and video (printed p. 18).
The report says average news-site referrals from Facebook fell 43% and from X fell 46% over the previous two and a half years (printed p. 18).

In “Where publishers plan to put more and less effort in 2026,” the net difference between plans for more and less effort was +74 for YouTube, +61 for AI platforms, and +56 for TikTok (printed p. 19).
sections.summary: Describes the shift from social sharing toward recommendation-driven feeds, video, and private messaging, and the resulting pressure on publisher referrals. It outlines publishers’ changing platform priorities and growing investment in video formats.
sections.title: 4. Social Media’s Mid-Life Crisis and the Video-fication of Everything

key_points: For the Q19 measure of respondents somewhat or very concerned, 70% cited creators taking time and attention away from publisher content, compared with 39% concerned about losing talent (printed p. 22).

In “Top planned publisher initiatives in response to the creator wave,” 76% planned to encourage journalists to behave more like creators, 50% to partner with creators for distribution, and 31% to hire creators (printed p. 23).
The section describes the risk that journalists who build independent profiles may leave with their audiences, including the example of former Washington Post creator Dave Jorgenson.
sections.summary: Explores creators as competitors for audience attention and editorial talent, while noting that publishers are also learning from creator-led approaches. It describes plans to adapt staff, partnerships, hiring, and studio models in response.
sections.title: 5. Responding to the Creator Wave

key_points: In “Publisher perceptions about whether misinformation and expansion of AI-generated content strengthen or weaken news media,” 52% said these trends could strengthen news media, 27% said weaken, and 15% said make no difference (printed p. 28).

The report says fewer than 1% of news images or videos published globally included C2PA metadata, and notes that TikTok’s automated detection may identify less than half of AI-generated content (printed p. 28).

The section describes more than 4,000 AI-powered fake news websites identified in France and cites a survey finding that four in ten respondents had encountered low-quality AI-generated workplace material during the previous month (printed p. 29).
sections.summary: Reviews the spread of AI-generated content and the use of manipulated media in political contexts, alongside uncertainty about the effects on trust and democracy. It discusses provenance standards, platform detection and labeling, AI content farms, and low-quality AI-generated workplace material.
sections.title: 6. AI Slop, Deep-Fakes, and Misinformation

key_points: In “Different uses of AI that will be important in 2026,” the share rating each use “very important” was 64% for back-end automation, 44% for coding and product development, 36% for distribution and recommendations, 33% for commercial uses, and 29% each for newsgathering and human-supervised content creation (printed p. 30).
In the chart on the impact of current newsroom AI initiatives, 44% described results as promising, 42% as limited, and 13% as transformational (printed p. 31).
In the chart on jobs saved or added as a result of AI initiatives, 67% reported no jobs cut, 16% a small number cut, and 9% jobs added (printed p. 31).
sections.summary: Examines publishers’ adoption of AI for efficiency and journalistic work, alongside concerns about chatbot accuracy and uneven results from newsroom initiatives. Examples include automation, coding, newsgathering, and AI-supported reporting and product development.
sections.title: 7. Latest Tales of AI in the Newsroom

key_points: In “Most important expected commercial publisher revenue streams in 2026,” the shares selecting subscription/membership, display advertising/sponsorship, native advertising, and events were 76%, 68%, 64%, and 54%, respectively (printed p. 36).
In the same chart, 37% selected funding from platforms, including AI platforms; the report notes this had risen 17 percentage points in two years (printed p. 36).
The section identifies lack of resources (62%), lack of skills (53% net), and internal competition between groups (49%) as barriers to innovation.
Predictions include further mergers and acquisitions and experimentation with community-participation models for local news.
sections.summary: Reviews pressures on established revenue models, publishers’ expectations for commercial income, and barriers to developing new products. It also considers consolidation and new approaches to local news.
sections.title: 8. Changing Business Models and Barriers to Innovation

key_points: In “Expected impact of new browsers and agentic apps,” respondents assessed impact over the next three years: 15% expected a very large impact and 60% a large impact on publishers (printed p. 39).
The report describes AI browsers and apps that can summarize or translate webpages, complete tasks, and assemble personalized news briefings.
It argues that more liquid content and agentic bots may make it harder to control how stories appear and to measure human visits.
sections.summary: Considers rapid change in AI browsers, agentic apps, and interfaces, and the implications of increasingly adaptable content for publishers’ control, measurement, and monetization. The section also raises the possibility of a stronger backlash against technology.
sections.title: 9. What’s Next in Technology?

sections.summary: The report’s concluding section closes its discussion of journalism and technology trends for 2026.
sections.title: 10. Conclusions

key_points: A closed online survey was completed by 280 senior publishing-industry participants from 51 countries and territories between 18 November and 20 December 2025 (printed p. 43).

Participants held editorial, commercial, or product roles and were responsible for aspects of digital or wider media strategy; the report cautions that the results are not representative of the wider industry.
sections.summary: Explains the survey sample and collection period, emphasizing that the responses reflect a strategic group of senior industry leaders rather than a representative sample. It also summarizes participant roles, organization types, and geographic coverage.
sections.title: Survey Methodology

doc_map.summary: Nic Newman’s report examines the pressures facing journalism and publishers in 2026, including AI-driven changes to search and content, competition from creators, platform shifts, misinformation, newsroom AI adoption, and business-model challenges. It draws on a survey of senior digital leaders and combines survey results with analysis and predictions for the year ahead.
doc_map.title: Journalism and Technology Trends and Predictions 2026

findings.evidence:
There are many other barriers to innovation. Six in ten (62%) of our respondents say that media companies simply aren’t investing enough in future models, citing lack of resources. There is also a skills problem, with around half (53%) identifying challenges in either attracting product people who can help define the right solutions, or the technical and design talent to deliver them.

The other big problem identified by our survey is alignment. Around a quarter (26%) think the top-level strategy is not sufficiently clear, with half (49%) complaining about internal competition between different groups which makes it hard to align different parts of the organisation around new projects.

limitations: Publisher expectations that misinformation and AI-generated content could strengthen news media may be wishful thinking; audience uncertainty about truth does not necessarily mean they will return to news media.
Fewer than 1% of news images or videos published globally include C2PA metadata; adoption requires ecosystem-wide buy-in, and metadata can be stripped at any stage.
Content-detection systems have so far been only partly effective; some experts suggest TikTok automatically detects less than half of AI-generated content.

methods: Industry survey of a strategic sample of 280 digital leaders from 51 countries and territories; question-specific bases include 273 respondents (Q9) and 264 (Q13).

Chartbeat analytics data on page-view referrals aggregated across more than 2,000 news websites and apps in its network; the report also describes aggregate Google Search traffic to hundreds of news sites.
Background conversations, interviews, and emails with publishers, academics, and industry experts provided additional input.

The fear is that human-generated, verified content will soon be drowned out by machine-made ‘AI slop’.

report_context.overview: Journalism and Technology Trends and Predictions 2026 by Reuters Institute for the Study of Journalism Nic Newman’s report examines the pressures facing journalism and publishers in 2026, including AI-driven changes to search and content, competition from creators, platform shifts, misinformation, newsroom AI adoption, and business-model challenges. It draws on a survey of senior digital leaders and combines survey results with analysis and predictions for the year ahead. Covers journalism and technology trends, challenges, and predictions for 2026, including AI, audience traffic, content and distribution strategies, misinformation, newsroom practices, and business models. Draws on an industry survey of digital leaders from 51 countries and territories; the excerpts do not identify specific geographic regions.

normalized_payload.commentary: Chartbeat aggregate data show Google traffic from organic search to more than 2,500 sites fell 33% globally from November 2024 to November 2025. For Q5, the 268 respondents’ average slider score was −43% on a slider ranging from +100% to −100%, indicating an expectation of declining search-engine traffic over the next three years. Among the 264 Q13 respondents, the reported net differences between proportions saying each area was more versus less important for newsroom focus in the era of AI were +91 for original investigations/on-the-ground reporting, +82 for contextual analysis (explanation, framing), and −42 for service journalism. Among Q11 respondents (base 265), 44% chose promising and 42% limited as the adjective closest to describing the impact of newsroom AI initiatives so far. Among publisher respondents (base 272), 69% expect possible licensing deals with AI companies around news-content IP to bring at least some income to their company in about three years: 49% expect a minor source and 20% a significant source.

insights: Chartbeat aggregate data sourced for the report show Google traffic from organic search to more than 2,500 sites fell 33% globally between November 2024 and November 2025. Separately, the average slider score among Q5 respondents (base 268; slider range +100% to −100%) was −43% for expected search-engine traffic change over the next three years, an expectation rather than an observed change.

Among the 264 Q13 respondents, the reported net difference between proportions saying areas were more versus less important for newsroom focus in the era of AI was +91 for original investigations/on-the-ground reporting, +82 for contextual analysis (explanation, framing), and −42 for service journalism.
Among respondents to Q19 (base 263), 70% were somewhat or very concerned about creators taking time and attention away from publisher content, compared with 39% concerned about losing talent.

Among respondents answering Q11 (base = 265), 44% chose promising, 42% limited, 13% transformational, and 2% disappointing as the adjective closest to describing the impact of newsroom AI initiatives so far.

Among publisher respondents (base 272), 69% expect possible licensing deals with AI companies around news-content IP to bring at least some money to their company in about three years: 49% expect a minor source and 20% a significant source. Separately, 20% expect no income, 11% don't know, and 0% expect a main source of income.

About the Author 
Nic Newman is Senior Research Associate at the Reuters Institute for the Study of Journalism 
where he was lead author of the annual Digital News Report 2012–25. He is also a consultant 
on digital media, working actively with news companies on product, audience, and business 
strategies. He has produced a media and journalism predictions report for almost 20 years. This 
is	the	tenth	to	be	published	by	the	Reuters	Institute.	Nic	was	a	founding	member	of	the	BBC	
News Website, leading international coverage as World Editor (1997–2001). As Head of Product 
Development (2001–10) he led digital teams, developing websites, mobile, and interactive TV 
applications	for	all	BBC	Journalism	sites.	
 
Acknowledgements
The	author	would	like	to	thank	280	news	executives	from	51	countries	and	territories	who	gave	
up their time to respond to our survey around the key challenges and opportunities in the year 
ahead. 
Respondents included 64 editors-in-chief, another 64 CEOs or managing directors, and 51 
heads of digital or innovation, and came from some of the world’s leading traditional media 
companies as well as digital-born organisations (see breakdown at the end of the report). 
Survey input and answers helped guide some of the themes in this report and data have been 
used throughout. Some direct quotes do not carry names or organisations, at the request of 
those contributors.

Development, and the wider team at the Institute for their ideas and suggestions, and to 
a range of other experts and news executives who generously contributed their time in 
background interviews (see full list at the end of this report). 
Thanks also go to Alex Reid for her input on the manuscript over the holiday season and 
keeping	the	publication	on	track.	As	with	many	predictions	reports	there	is	a	significant

in mind. Having said that, any mistakes – factual or otherwise – should be considered entirely 
the responsibility of the author.

3
JOURNALISM AND TECHNOLOGY TRENDS AND PREDICTIONS 2026
Executive Summary 
We are still at the early stages of another big shift in technology (Generative AI) which 
threatens	to	upend	the	news	industry	by	offering	more	efficient	ways	of	accessing	and	distilling	
information	at	scale.	At	the	same	time,	creators	and	influencers	(humans)	are	driving	a	shift	
towards personality-led news, at the expense of media institutions that can often feel less 
relevant, less interesting, and less authentic. In 2026 the news media are likely to be further 
squeezed by these two powerful forces. 
Understanding the impact of these trends, and working out how to combat them, will be high 
up the ‘to do list’ of media executives this year, despite the unevenly distributed pace of change 
across countries and demographics.
Existential challenges abound. Declining engagement for traditional media combined with 
low trust is leading many politicians, businessmen, and celebrities to conclude that they can 
bypass the media entirely, giving interviews instead to sympathetic podcasters or YouTubers. 
This Trump 2.0 playbook – now widely copied around the world – often comes bundled with a 
barrage of intimidating legal threats against publishers and continuing attempts to undermine 
trust by branding independent media and individual journalists as ‘fake news’. These 
narratives	are	finding	fertile	ground	with	audiences	–	especially	younger	ones	–	that	prefer	the	
convenience of accessing news from platforms, and have weaker connections with traditional 
news brands. Meanwhile search engines are turning into AI-driven answer engines, where 
content	is	surfaced	in	chat	windows,	raising	fears	that	referral	traffic	for	publishers	could	dry	
up, undermining existing and future business models.
Despite	these	difficulties	many	traditional	news	organisations	remain	optimistic	about	their	
own business – if not about journalism itself. Publishers will be focused this year on re-
engineering their businesses for the age of AI, with more distinctive content and a more human 
face. They will also be looking beyond the article, investing more in multiple formats especially 
video and adjusting their content to make it more ‘liquid’ and therefore easier to reformat and 
personalise. At the same time, they’ll be continuing to work out how best to use Generative AI 
themselves across newsgathering, packaging, and distribution. It’s a delicate balancing act but 
one	that	–	if	they	can	pull	it	off	–	holds	out	the	promise	of	greater	efficiency	and	more	relevant	
and engaging journalism.
How media leaders view the year ahead
These	are	the	main	findings	from	our	industry	survey,	drawn	from	a	strategic	sample	of	280	
digital leaders from 51 countries and territories: 
• Only	slightly	more	than	a	third	(38%)	of	our	sample	of	editors,	CEOs,	and	digital	
executives	say	they	are	confident	about	the	prospects	for	journalism	in	the	year	ahead	
– that’s 22pp lower than four years ago. Stated concerns relate to politically motivated 
attacks on journalism, loss of USAID money that previously supported independent media 
in	many	parts	of	the	world,	and	significant	declines	in	traffic	to	many	online	news	sites.
